To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Wolbachia strains infecting Culex pipien mosquitoes in La Réunion belong all to the same genetic group, but that they can nevertheless be divided into five distinct groups based on their compatibility properties.
the CI properties of Wolbachia are controlled by several factors and that these factors are not linked to the nuclear background of the host.

Wolbachia from La Réunion mosquito populations are all mutually compatible but belong to at least 5 distinct incompatibility types, which formally establishes that CI is controlled by multiple Wolbachia mod/esc factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular basis of the cytoplasmic compatibility between Wolbachia strains in the mosquito Culex pipien s.
understanding the genetic basis of Wolbachia‐induced cytoplasmic compatibility in mosquitoes.
the genetic and evolutionary aspects of Wolbachia infections and their impact on arthropod populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CI phenotype is controlled by at least five Wolbachia genes, each of which is involved in a distinct CI pathway.
the CI phenotype of wPip is determined by a combination of several Wolbachia genes, which are not necessarily linked and are not necessarily present in the same wPip strain.
CI in Culex mosquitoes is controlled by a complex of at least five Wolbachia genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolution of Wolbachia CI in C. pipienes is controlled by at least six different factors.
Wolbachia are able to manipulate their host's reproduction by using a large number of different factors, which can be considered as a form of molecular redundancy.
the wPip strains from La Réunions belong to five distinct incompatibly groups (or crossing groups).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the wPip genetic diversity in C. pipien s populations is the result of a long‐term co‐evolution between Wolbachia and their hosts.
Wolbachia mod and resc factors are not randomly distributed in natural populations, but instead are organized into distinct incompatibility groupings.
Wolbachia mod factors are not unique to each Wolbachia strain but rather are present in several copies, and that their evolution is not constrained by their genetic relatedness.
